prompt: You compare analogue-style all-pole low-pass designs of order one and four, well into their stopbands and away from digital Nyquist effects. What should you expect?

options.text: The one-pole design suppresses distant harmonics more steeply
options.explanation: Under the stated asymptotic rule, more poles give a steeper stopband.

options.text: Both behave as brick walls at cutoff
options.explanation: These responses roll off gradually; cutoff is a reference point.

options.text: The four-pole design has a steeper stopband, but its exact response still depends on design
options.explanation: Correct. Pole count gives the qualified asymptotic trend, not every detail of a digital response.

options.text: The pole count alone specifies resonance and phase at every frequency
options.explanation: Pole count does not fully specify pole locations, zeros or response shape.

workedExample: Each pole contributes additional attenuation as frequency rises in the stated all-pole asymptotic region. More poles therefore produce a steeper distant roll-off. Near cutoff or Nyquist, inspect the actual design rather than extending the rule blindly.

link.title: Introduction to digital filters — Julius O. Smith

prompt: A low-pass is advertised with a 24 dB-per-octave asymptotic slope. Can you infer its exact gain near cutoff simply by extending that straight line?

options.text: Yes: the asymptote is the exact curve everywhere
options.explanation: An asymptote describes a limiting trend, not the entire response.

options.text: No: cutoff shape and resonance can differ substantially; use the actual response
options.explanation: Correct. The straight-line rule is intended well into the stopband under the stated design assumptions.

options.text: Yes, provided the output signal is quieter
options.explanation: Changing signal level does not make the asymptotic approximation exact for an LTI filter.

options.text: No filter can attenuate frequencies above cutoff gradually
options.explanation: Gradual attenuation is precisely what the response curve describes.

workedExample: The slope says how much additional rejection accumulates per frequency doubling in the asymptotic region. It does not specify the cutoff neighbourhood, resonance or digital behaviour near Nyquist. Use a frequency response calculation or settled-tone measurement for an exact requirement.
